name: Butyrate supplements taken by mouth (mostly sodium butyrate)
short: Some children with congenital chloride diarrhoea had worse diarrhoea on sodium butyrate. Trials: mild nausea and headache in 2 children (54-child obesity trial); none in a 72-child IBD trial.
text: These data are for butyrate, mostly as sodium butyrate, taken by mouth. In children with congenital chloride diarrhoea, a 2021 report states in its background that butyrate seems not to be well tolerated by all patients, with some reporting worse diarrhoea. It describes three children whose diarrhoea worsened or did not improve on sodium butyrate at 100 mg/kg/day; in all three, the report's step-up approach, with a gradual weekly increase, then limited diarrhoea severity. In a 6-month quadruple-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 54 children with obesity, transient mild nausea and headache were reported by 2 patients during the first month of butyrate; the abstract does not give the size of the butyrate group. In a 12-week placebo-controlled trial in children and adolescents with newly diagnosed inflammatory bowel disease (72 completed: 29 on sodium butyrate, 43 on placebo), none of the patients reported adverse events. In a 6-week placebo-controlled trial in 42 adults with type 2 diabetes, total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol and insulin rose significantly from baseline with sodium butyrate, although the differences from placebo were not significant; the authors describe no or even adverse changes in some blood measures. In a 4-week placebo-controlled trial in adults with chronic urticaria (29 completed), all also taking bilastine, the authors describe butyrate as safe, without giving adverse-event numbers. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
